headline: Connecticut releases guide to new 250-foot election security zone
dek: The public guide explains how a new law limits law-enforcement activity and certain conduct near polling places, early-voting sites and ballot drop boxes before the Nov. 3 general election.
body: Connecticut election officials have released a public guide explaining a new 250-foot security zone around election sites, giving voters, registrars and law-enforcement agencies a common reference before the state’s Nov. 3 general election. Secretary of the State Stephanie Thomas and Department of Emergency Services and Public Protection Commissioner Ronnell Higgins announced the guide Oct. 15 as part of a broader effort to prepare for Election Day. The [Secretary of the State’s announcement](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/press-releases/2026-press-releases/secretary-thomas-despp-highlight-election-preparations-release-250-foot-election-security-rule-guide) says the resource is meant to translate the law into practical instructions.

The rule reaches beyond the doorway of a traditional polling place. The state says the guide covers polling locations, early-voting sites, same-day voter-registration locations, absentee-ballot drop boxes and other designated election sites. That matters because voters may encounter different rules depending on whether they are casting a ballot on Nov. 3, voting early or using an absentee process. The guide is intended to explain where the perimeter starts, when it is active and how possible violations should be reported.

Public Act 26-42 generally bars covered officers and agents authorized by a state or the federal government to use force, search, detain or arrest people from knowingly entering or remaining within the 250-foot perimeter. The law also restricts those officers from checking voter qualifications or loitering in the zone, subject to exceptions. Connecticut’s official [election-services guidance](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/election-services/public-act-26-42/250-ft-signage) describes the rule’s definitions and exceptions, including situations involving an immediate threat to life or property, a court-authorized action with advance notice, or permission from the secretary of the state or an election moderator.

The law is not a ban on every police activity near a voting location. The new state guide says officers may still conduct routine patrols, enforce traffic laws and respond to emergencies. It also addresses the circumstances in which law-enforcement personnel may be present for a specific duty, as well as how long they may remain. That distinction is central to the rollout: election officials must protect access to the ballot while public-safety agencies retain a way to respond when an urgent incident occurs.

The guide also explains a separate face-covering provision. State officials say people generally may not wear a mask within the 250-foot perimeter when it obscures the face, head or identity, with exceptions tied to religion, medical necessity or weather. The Secretary of the State’s release says the guide includes information about identification requirements and reporting possible violations. Voters should check the official material or ask local election officials about questions that depend on the specific site or activity.

Connecticut officials say the public document follows months of coordination rather than a last-minute rule change. The Secretary of the State’s office has worked with the Connecticut Intelligence Center, local law-enforcement partners and the Connecticut Police Chiefs Association. It has also used regular calls with registrars and plans additional interagency training involving the State Elections Enforcement Commission, the attorney general’s office and the Division of Criminal Justice, according to the state announcement.

The need for a practical explanation became clearer during the summer. [Connecticut Public reported](https://www.ctpublic.org/news/2026-08-28/a-state-law-restricting-banning-police-at-polling-sites-creates-confusion-and-division-in-fairfield) that officials in Fairfield and other communities worried the new distance requirement could be difficult to apply during ordinary calls, while supporters said the law was designed to prevent intimidation by immigration-enforcement agents. That report also described the change as an expansion from the state’s previous 75-foot electioneering boundary to a 250-foot law-enforcement restriction. The concerns were reported before the state issued its voter-facing guide; the guide is the administration’s effort to clarify how the enacted law should work.

The first statewide general election under the new framework will show whether the written exceptions and local training resolve those concerns in practice. Connecticut’s Secretary of the State directs voters to [MyVote.CT.gov](https://myvote.ct.gov/) for general-election information, while the new guide provides the details for the 250-foot zone. What remains unknown is how often municipalities will need to use the exceptions, how many complaints will be filed and whether lawmakers will seek further changes after Nov. 3. For now, the state’s message is that voters should be able to reach election sites without intimidation, and officials should understand the limits and responsibilities that apply around them.
author: NorthEast News Desk
